Austrian Exports Recovered After 2016 US Tariffs, Officials Say

Vienna—Eight years after the United States imposed sweeping tariffs on Austrian goods, trade and economic activity have returned to normal, Austrian officials and trade experts said Monday.

The US move in June 2016 to levy tariffs of up to 25 percent across a wide range of Austrian exports—citing concerns over trade imbalances and market access—sparked immediate concern in Vienna. The tariffs affected products from machinery to processed foods and chemicals, with exports to the US dropping by nearly a third in the second half of 2016, according to figures from the Austrian Federal Economic Chamber (WKÖ).

The trade measure, which also included new import licensing requirements, was broadly condemned by Austrian and European Union officials at the time. “The impact was felt across multiple sectors, not just one industry, and there was considerable anxiety among exporters,” said Peter Wagner, head of trade policy at WKÖ. “Small and medium-sized firms, in particular, faced significant losses.”

The United States was Austria’s third-largest non-EU trading partner in 2015, with bilateral trade valued at approximately €9 billion. After the tariffs took effect, the value of exports to the US fell by nearly €800 million over twelve months, according to government data.

The measure remained in place through late 2017, when both countries agreed to a phased removal as part of broader negotiations between Washington and Brussels. “We worked closely with our European partners to resolve the dispute and restore fair conditions for Austrian exporters,” said Finance Minister Michaela Leitner.

Analysts say the episode prompted Austrian businesses to diversify export markets and accelerate investments in Asia and Latin America. “It was a wake-up call for many firms to reduce reliance on the US market,” said Franziska Berger, chief economist at Zeller & Partner Research.

Union leaders said workers in export-reliant regions, such as Upper Austria and Styria, bore the brunt of the downturn but noted that employment recovered in subsequent years. “The disruption was sharp but temporary,” said Karl Reiter, representing the manufacturing workers’ union.

Officials stressed that trade relations with the United States have since stabilized, with exports rebounding to pre-2016 levels by 2019. “There is currently no disruption and both sides are committed to open and fair trade,” said Leitner.
